land.text: 'In the mountains near Sidi Rafaa' (Bayda) he built the Zawiya Bayda "White Monastery"', the order's first seat in Libya

predecessors.note: De facto only: the Ottomans never ceded land to the order, whose seat they kept under 'direct Ottoman surveillance' (Senussi page); the order grew inside the Ottoman vilayets of Tripoli and Benghazi until the Treaty of Ouchy (1912).

land.text: what was left of the Senussi land when 'Badoglio proclaimed the end of the campaign' in January 1932: Cyrenaica beyond the coastal lowlands, Jaghbub and Kufra, which had fallen in 1926 and 1931

successors.note: italian-africa (the umbrella) records the same hand-over in its ledger 40; Italian Libya is the colony that held Cyrenaica.

capitals.name: Bayda (Zawiya Bayda, Sidi Rafaa')
capitals.note: The order's seat after Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi returned to Libya in 1843; the page gives no year for building the zawiya.

capitals.name: Jaghbub
capitals.note: 'In 1855, the Sanusi order moved farther from direct Ottoman surveillance to Jaghbub'; the Jaghbub page has the capital there 'from 1856 to 1895'.

capitals.name: Jawf (Jof), Kufra oases
capitals.note: Headquarters moved to 'Jof in the oases of Kufra in 1894' (Senussi page; the Kufra page says 1895). The pages do not say when Kufra ceased to be the headquarters; the Italians took Kufra in 1931 (Kufra page), so 1931 is the last year.

rulers.name: Muhammad ibn Ali as-Senussi (the Grand Senussi)
rulers.note: The page's leader list; 'Senussi ended up dying in Jaghbub in 1859' (Jaghbub page).

rulers.name: Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi
rulers.note: The page's list gives 1902-1916, but the text has Idris replacing him as effective leader in 1917 and Ahmed's leadership 'mostly nominal' from 1917 to his death in 1933.

rulers.name: Idris (later King Idris of Libya)
rulers.title: Head of the order; Emir of Cyrenaica from October 1920
rulers.note: The list gives 1916-1969; the dossier stops at 1932. Idris was in exile in Egypt from 1922 (page).

correction.text: 'In the mountains near Sidi Rafaa' (Bayda) he built the Zawiya Bayda "White Monastery"', after he 'returned to Libya' in 1843

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: a 50 km disc round Al Bayda stands for the Zawiya Bayda in the Jebel Akhdar. The page gives no territory, area or infobox figure (its infobox has only 'Key people' and 'Part of'), so the disc is a placeholder for the order's seat, not a measured border.

correction.text: Bayda and the Jaghbub oasis, 'a small oasis some 30 miles northwest of Siwa'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the Bayda disc plus an 80 km disc round Jaghbub oasis, where the order settled in 1855. The page gives no area; the 80 km radius is the researcher's.

correction.text: Bayda, Jaghbub and 'Jof in the oases of Kufra'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: adds the Kufra oases (a 150 km disc round Al Jawf, the 'Jof' of the page) after the 1894 move. The page says the oases from Siwa to Kufra and Borkou 'were cultivated by the Sanusi order' and that al-Mahdi 'had the authority of a sovereign in a vast but almost empty desert', but dates and bounds none of it; the shape holds the three seats only.

correction.text: inland Cyrenaica outside the coastal enclaves: 'After the Treaty of Ouchy, the Senussi order controlled most of Libya'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: after the Treaty of Ouchy (18 October 1912) 'the Senussi order controlled most of Libya' while 'the Italian soldiers were in effect besieged in seven enclaves on the coasts of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica' (the Cyrenaican ones drawn as 15 km discs round Tobruk, Derna and Benghazi; Cyrene joins them by 1915). The shape is the gazetteer's Cyrenaica minus those enclaves: the Pacification page's 'large swaths of the interior remained under local Libyan rule' and the Senussi page's 'most of inland Cyrenaica under the de facto control of the Senussis' support Cyrenaica, not Tripolitania or the Fezzan. No infobox area exists to compare.

correction.text: inland Cyrenaica without the northern lowlands the Italians 'regained' in 1923-1924

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: 'From 1923 to 1924 ... they also regained the northern lowlands of Cyrenaica', so the coastal plain (the Benghazi and Marj districts, a stand-in: the page names no district) leaves the shape while 'attempts to occupy the forested hills of Jebel Akhtar were met with strong guerrilla resistance'. The 1920 accord had the Senussi administering 'the oases around Kufra, Jalu, Jaghbub, Awjila, and Ajdabiya', all of which stay inside.

correction.text: inland Cyrenaica without the northern lowlands and without Jaghbub, occupied by the Italians in early 1926

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Jaghbub leaves the shape. 'Around early 1926, with the help of the Frontier Wire, the Italians were able to successfully occupy Jaghbub' (the oasis had been transferred to Italy by the Italian-Egyptian treaty of 6 December 1925).

correction.text: inland Cyrenaica without the northern lowlands, Jaghbub and Kufra

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Kufra leaves the shape: 'In 1931, during the campaign of Cyrenaica, General Rodolfo Graziani easily conquered Kufra'. What remains is the interior the Second Italo-Senussi War page shows as still resisting (Jebel Akhdar and the Awjila-Ajdabiya oases) until Badoglio's proclamation in January 1932; the pages do not say when those districts fell, so they stay inside the shape.

region.text: 'In the mountains near Sidi Rafaa' (Bayda) he built the Zawiya Bayda "White Monastery"'

ledger.note: 1843: Muhammad ibn Ali as-Senussi returns to Libya and builds the Zawiya Bayda in the Jebel Akhdar. 'In 1843 the Wahhabis forced him to leave the area and he returned to Libya'; the order 'was founded in Mecca in 1837'. The page dates the return, not the building of the zawiya, and the land is a disc round Bayda; the Ottomans stayed nominal sovereigns.
1855: the order moves its seat to Jaghbub. 'In 1855, the Sanusi order moved farther from direct Ottoman surveillance to Jaghbub' (the Jaghbub page says 'by 1856' and a capital 'from 1856 to 1895').

region.text: Jaghbub, 'a small oasis some 30 miles northwest of Siwa'

ledger.note: 1855: the Senussi settle Jaghbub oasis. The page names no state that held it (counterpart nobody is the researcher's reading); Italy later got it from Egypt by the treaty of 6 December 1925 (Jaghbub page).

1894: the headquarters moves to Kufra. After the 1889 visit of the pasha of Benghazi 'accompanied by Ottoman troops', the leader moved 'his headquarters to Jof in the oases of Kufra in 1894' (the Kufra page: 'In 1895 seeking greater independence the Senussi relocated from Jaghbub, making the oasis their main centre').

1894: the Senussi take up the Kufra oases. 'In most of Tripoli and Benghazi his authority was greater than that of the Ottoman governors' and 'Muhammed al-Mahdi had the authority of a sovereign in a vast but almost empty desert' (undated). The page names no other state on the oases.

region.text: inland Cyrenaica outside the coastal enclaves

ledger.note: October 1912: the Senussi hold the Cyrenaican interior as the Ottomans leave. 'After the Treaty of Ouchy, the Senussi order controlled most of Libya' (treaty of 18 October 1912); 'The Italian soldiers were in effect besieged in seven enclaves on the coasts of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica.' De facto control, not a cession; the Cyrenaican reading of 'most of Libya' is the researcher's.

region.text: the interior of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica beyond the coastal enclaves

ledger.note: October 1912: the interior stays out of Italian hands. The Senussi order, which refused to surrender, 'controlled most of Libya'; Italy had declared its sovereignty by 'a decree of 5 November 1911'; 'The Italian control over much of the interior of Libya remained ineffective until the late 1920s.' Region copied from italian-africa ledger 16; the page names no Tripolitanian district, and the Tripolitanian part of the zone is doubtful (see notes).

region.text: the interior of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica beyond the coastal enclaves

ledger.note: 1917: the Treaty of Acroma. 'In 1917, the Treaty of Acroma was signed between the UK, Italy and the Senussis'; the Senussis 'repudiated Ottoman authority' and were recognised 'an autonomy that was tantamount to effective independence'; 'Conflict between the British and the Senussis continued until 1917.' The Accord of al-Rajma of October 1920 then gave Idris the title Emir of Cyrenaica and the autonomous administration of 'the oases around Kufra, Jalu, Jaghbub, Awjila, and Ajdabiya'; neither moves a border on the pages.

region.text: the Jebel Akhdar and interior of Cyrenaica, the Senussi homeland

ledger.note: 26 January 1923: the Second Italo-Senussi War begins. Infobox '26 January 1923 - 24 January 1932', location 'Italian Tripolitania, Italian Cyrenaica', fighting 'most intense and prolonged in the mountainous Jebel Akhdar region of Cyrenaica'. Region as in italian-libya ledger 9.
26 January 1923: the Cyrenaica war begins (the same event as the italian-libya pair, recorded against the umbrella as italian-africa ledger 22 does). Infobox '26 January 1923 - 24 January 1932'.

1923-1924: Italy retakes the coastal plain. 'In that period, they also regained the northern lowlands of Cyrenaica'; 'attempts to occupy the forested hills of Jebel Akhtar were met with strong guerrilla resistance.' The page names no district; the Benghazi and Marj districts are the researcher's stand-in. The Sirtica gain of 1924 ('150,000 square kilometres in five months') is recorded by italian-libya as nobody's land.

Early 1926: the Italians occupy Jaghbub. 'Around early 1926, with the help of the Frontier Wire, the Italians were able to successfully occupy Jaghbub'; 'a treaty was signed between Italy and Egypt which transferred Jaghbub to Italy on December 6, 1925' (italian-africa ledger 32 records that cession as a gain from kingdom-of-egypt).

1931: Graziani conquers Kufra. 'In 1931, during the campaign of Cyrenaica, General Rodolfo Graziani easily conquered Kufra' with about 3,000 troops and some twenty bombers; refugees 'fled into the desert' (the Graziani sentence is the Kufra page's; the Second Italo-Senussi War page has 'In 1931, Italian forces seized Kufra'). italian-libya ledger 13 and italian-africa ledger 38 record the same land as a gain from nobody.

region.text: the Jebel Akhdar and interior of Cyrenaica, the Senussi homeland

ledger.note: January 1932: the last Cyrenaican resistance ends. 'In January 1932, Badoglio proclaimed the end of the campaign' (infobox end 24 January 1932); Mukhtar was 'wounded and then captured' in September 1931 and executed at Suluq.
January 1932: the Cyrenaica war ends (the umbrella's pair of italian-africa ledger 39). 'Mukhtar's death effectively ended the resistance.'

region.text: what remained of the Senussi land: Cyrenaica beyond the coastal lowlands, Jaghbub and Kufra

ledger.note: January 1932: Cyrenaica passes under Italian control. Infobox result 'Italian victory'; 'in January 1932, Badoglio proclaimed the end of the campaign'. The page says the campaign ended, not that every district was held; the Cyrenaican camps ('well over half the population of Cyrenaica' confined by 1931) closed in September 1933.

region.text: what remained of the Senussi land

ledger.note: January 1932: the same hand-over recorded against the umbrella, as italian-africa ledger 40 does.

region.text: what remained of the Senussi land

ledger.note: January 1932: the Senussi state ends in Cyrenaica. 'Mukhtar's death effectively ended the resistance'; Idris had been in exile in Egypt since 1922 and Ahmed Sharif's leadership was 'mostly nominal' from 1917 (Senussi page). The order itself and the Emirate of Cyrenaica (a separate dossier, 1949-1951) outlive this.

wars.name: Italo-Senussi hostilities after the Treaty of Ouchy

zones.text: the interior of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica beyond the coastal enclaves

wars.outcome: The Italians were confined to coastal enclaves: 'besieged in seven enclaves' at the end of 1912 and, 'by 1 August 1915', concentrated in Tripoli, Homs, Benghazi, Derna, Cyrene and Tobruk. The Treaty of Acroma (1917) recognised Senussi autonomy.
wars.note: Not an article title: a descriptive name. The Italo-Turkish War page gives the siege and the 1915 withdrawal but no battle; the Senussi page calls the 1915-1917 period 'guerrilla warfare against the Italian colonization of Libya'.

wars.name: Senussi Campaign
wars.outcome: The order fought 'in Egypt from November 1915 until February 1917' and 'in the Sudan from March to December 1916'; 'the British sent an expeditionary force against them known as the Senussi Campaign'. Ended by the Treaty of Acroma of 1917.
wars.note: No border moved on the pages; the Senussi page gives these dates and nothing of the ground held.

wars.name: Second Italo-Senussi War

zones.text: the Jebel Akhdar and interior of Cyrenaica, the Senussi homeland

wars.outcome: Italian victory: the northern lowlands regained in 1923-1924, Jaghbub occupied early 1926, Kufra seized 1931, Mukhtar captured September 1931 and executed, Badoglio proclaims the end of the campaign in January 1932.
wars.note: Infobox 26 January 1923 - 24 January 1932. The war also covers the Italian reconquest of Tripolitania and the Fezzan (1930), which are the italian-libya dossier's contests with the Tripolitanian Republic, not the Senussi.

certainty.note: No page gives a boundary for the order's land: the early shapes are discs round its seats, the later ones the gazetteer's Cyrenaica less the places the pages say fell. Even the Italian-Egyptian treaty of 6 December 1925 (Jaghbub) was drawn by neither party's survey on the pages opened.

sources.title: Senussi
sources.note: Identity, founding (Mecca 1837, Libya 1843), seats (Bayda, Jaghbub 1855, Kufra 1894), leaders, Acroma 1917, al-Rajma 1920, Idris's exile 1922. No area, no infobox dates.

sources.title: Second Italo-Senussi War
sources.note: The war's dates (26 January 1923 - 24 January 1932), the northern lowlands, the 1920 accord's oases, Kufra 1931, Badoglio January 1932.

sources.title: Pacification of Libya
sources.note: 1911-1912 interior under local rule, Treaty of Acroma 1917, Accord of al-Rajma October 1920; the page reads as the same article as the Second Italo-Senussi War.

sources.title: Italo-Turkish War
sources.note: Treaty of Ouchy 18 October 1912, the Senussi order controlling most of Libya, the seven Italian enclaves, the 1915 withdrawal.

sources.title: Kufra
sources.note: Senussi centre from 1895, Italian conquest of Kufra in 1931 (Graziani).

sources.title: Jaghbub
sources.note: Senussi capital from 1856 to 1895, transfer to Italy on 6 December 1925, Italian occupation around early 1926.

notes: No Cliopatria row exists for the Senussi, so every keyframe is new and every shape is built from named places and the gazetteer's Cyrenaica; no page gives the order's territory or an infobox area, so there is no area comparison. Six pages opened (Senussi, Second Italo-Senussi War, Pacification of Libya, Italo-Turkish War, Kufra, Jaghbub); the Pacification page returned the same text as the Second Italo-Senussi War. Not settled: (1) the Tripolitanian half of the 1912-1917 contest zone (italian-africa ledger 16) rests on the Italo-Turkish page's 'controlled most of Libya'; the Tripolitanian interior was not Senussi land on any page, and the Tripolitanian Republic of 1918-1922 is a separate state, so the rendering agent may restrict that contest to Cyrenaica. (2) The Accord of al-Rajma (October 1920; Idris 'Emir of Cyrenaica'; Italy to police and administer the areas under Senussi control) is a recognition of Senussi autonomy under Italian sovereignty, with no territorial event for the map; it is in the 1917 event note and in the keyframe 1912-1923. (3) The Jaghbub page's summary of a Senussi return to Jaghbub in 1928 contradicts its own 1926 occupation and the Kufra page's 1931 conquest; not used. (4) The Senussi page dates the move to Kufra 1894, the Kufra page 1895; 1894 used. (5) Senussi fighting with the French in Chad and Wadai (the page: 'The Senussi kept them from advancing north of Chad', undated), the Borkou and Tibesti oases, and Fezzan are not dated on any page opened, so none is on the map; a gap-filler should open the Wikipedia articles on the French conquest of Chad and the Senussi-French conflict. (6) Which districts of the Awjila-Ajdabiya oases fell and when between 1926 and 1932 is page-silent. The Senussi are not a dynasty: Idris became King of Libya (1951) and the Emirate of Cyrenaica (1949-1951) has its own dossier. The Jaghbub (1925) cession from Egypt is in italian-africa ledger 32; italian-libya ledger 13 and italian-africa ledger 38 treat Kufra as nobody's land in 1931 and could name senussi-order instead.
